newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish government in corruption vote test.
newsitem.headline: Turkish government in corruption vote test.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist-led coalition faced a test of unity under growing strain on Thursday in votes on whether to impeach Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller on corruption charges.
Ciller, who is also foreign minister, looked set to avoid opposition bids to send her to the Supreme Court on two counts but the margin of the government majorities was likely to be tight.

Only hours ahead of the vote, a member of Ciller's True Path Party, deputy Mehmet Korkmaz, resigned. The opposition had been six short of the 276 MPs needed to impeach Ciller but it was not clear what way Korkmaz would vote.
Any breaks in coalition solidarity at the ballots would add to tensions within the administration, already at one of its lowest points since its formation last June.
A parliamentary session beginning at 1500 (1300 GMT) was to hear accusations Ciller was involved in graft during her three years as Turkey's first woman prime minister, from 1993.
A leading member of coalition partner Welfare Party, predicted the coalition would emerge intact.
"There's no reason for panic. This government has a lot more good work ahead of it," deputy Sevki Yilmaz told reporters.
But parliamentary sources said some deputies from Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's Welfare might stay away from the votes to avoid accusations of double standards.
The Islamists when in opposition had brought the charges last year in a successful bid to topple Ciller's partnership with fellow conservatives.
U.S.-educated technocrat Ciller is accused of illegally interfering with the sale of state-owned carmaker TOFAS and failing to prevent graft at the TEDAS electricity company.

The opposition must rely on defections from the Islamists or dissenters among her True Path Party. Some of Ciller's ministers have publicly criticised a recent bid by Erbakan to increase the role of Islam in public life.
The coalition is also under pressure from a tide of street demonstrations that started as protests at a security scandal but have turned into displays of general dissent.
The interior ministry has ordered provincial governors to take security measures against potential trouble at the nightly protests, Anatolian news agency said.
"As it is seems such protests will continue for a time...I request that all necessary security arrangements and measures be taken," it quoted Interior Minister Meral Aksener as saying.
Many Turks switch off their lights, sound car horns or take to the streets with lighted candles each night at nine p.m. (1900 GMT) for demonstrations dubbed "One minute's darkness for enligthenment."
Ciller faces a further corruption vote, on the source of her substantial personal wealth, in parliament on Wednesday. The government must also deal with an opposition censure motion next week.
